'''Alfred Wilhelm Hübler''' (May 16, 1957 – January 27, 2018) was a German-born research physicist at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]] (UIUC) [[Frederick Seitz|Frederick Seitz Materials Research Laboratory]] as well as a tenured faculty member in the University of Illinois Department of Physics. He was the director of the Center for Complex Systems Research (CCSR) and an external faculty member of the [[Santa Fe Institute]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.news-gazette.com/obituaries/2018-01-31/alfred-hubler.html|title=Alfred Hubler|website=news-gazette.com|access-date=2 February 2018}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Alfred Hübler was born in [[Munich]], [[West Germany]] in 1957. He received his diploma in 1983 and Ph.D. in 1987, [[Latin honors|summa cum laude]], from the Department of Physics, [[Technical University of Munich]]. His Ph.D. research was on controlling chaos and fractal particle agglomeration processes. After his Ph.D., Hubler joined [[Hermann Haken]]'s [[synergetics (Haken)|synergetics]] group at the [[University of Stuttgart]] as a post doctoral researcher.

Hübler became a faculty member of the Department of Physics at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1989.  He was also a long-time external faculty member of New Mexico's Santa Fe Institute. From 1993 to 1994, he was a Toshiba chair professor at [[Keio University]] in Tokio, Japan. He was Executive Editor of the journal ''[[Complexity (journal)|Complexity]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Complexity|doi=10.1002/(issn)1099-0526|doi-access=free|journal=Complexity }}</ref>

Hübler published more than 50 papers in peer-reviewed journals about his experimental and theoretical research on complex systems. His 2008 publication, entitled "''A simple, low-cost data-logging pendulum built from a computer mouse''" <ref name=Phys.Educ.>{{cite journal| author=V. Gintautas| author2=A. Hübler |title=A simple, low-cost data-logging pendulum built from a computer mouse|journal=Physics Education|year=2009 |volume=44 |issue=5|pages=488–491 |doi=10.1088/0031-9120/44/5/006|arxiv = 0901.4319 |bibcode = 2009PhyEd..44..488G |s2cid=56376026}}</ref> is one of the most downloaded papers of all [[Institute of Physics]] journal articles (in the top 3%). The [[American Physical Society]] (APS) listed his paper on [[mixed reality]] on the APS tipsheet and invited him to give a press conference on this topic at the 2008 March meeting. Hübler has a 1997 US patent on minimum dissipation quantum-dot transistors and in 2009 the UIUC filed a patent in his name on digital quantum batteries.

Hübler died in 2018 from [[lymphoma]].<ref name="illinois_obit">{{cite web | url=https://physics.illinois.edu/people/memorials/24474 | title=Alfred Wilhelm Hubler 1957-2018 | website=[[University of Illinois]]}}</ref>

== Research interests ==
Concepts governing the dynamics and structure of emergent patterns in open dissipative systems; mixed reality; prediction and control of fractal [[network dynamics]]; entrainment of cancer cells; energy conversion, storage, and distribution; dissipate wave-particle systems; solitons; homeopathy;<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1002/cplx.20220 | volume=13 | issue=3 | title="Homeopathic" dynamical systems | journal=Complexity | pages=8–11 | author=Hübler Alfred W|bibcode = 2008Cmplx..13c...8H | year=2008 | citeseerx=10.1.1.687.7950 }}</ref>
flames and shock waves; turbulence; reverse osmosis and filtration with fractal absorbers; conceptual networks; quantitative measures for knowledge and intelligence; natural language parsing.
